title: Need suggestions for AI sprite generation
author: jediwhiteshark
selftext:
I'm working on a 2D platformer and generated a few sprites for the character movement using Chatgpt. 

But later on when I asked for a few more sprites for the same character, it would never get me the correct sprites. It would add a few details like a small badge or an additional knee guard, despite prompting it not to add any detail or generate extra stuff. 

I'm not a developer and making this game purely using vibe code approach. 

I'm creating the game in Claude and sprite generation with ChatGPT.

comments.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
comments.body:
It will never get you consistent sprites. For small corrections within the same sprite, you need something that can do inpainting, for example Pixellab can do it.

For best consistency, you generate 3D models, rig them, animate them and then use AI to screencap the motions to create 100% consistent sprites.

replies.body: My game is a pixel art 2d platformer.

replies.author: EtadanikM
replies.body: Doesn’t matter, AI thinks in code and math, not like an artist, so to create animations it needs 3D models and movement definitions. It can’t “draw.”

replies.author: Suspicious_Bet3623
replies.body: Ludo.ai is extremely good at consistent sprites.  It will animate a sprite, change its direction, replace parts and more.

replies.author: Suspicious_Bet3623
replies.body:
No affiliation whatsoever.  I just asked google AI a few weeks ago what's best and it was an offered solution.

I'm doing a 2d point and click game which it isn't great at because it still fails to connect path tiles or seperate images seamlessly, but you can work with it by using the image editor and telling it to, for example, draw a winding path between the trees of a reference image and it'll do a good job most of the time.

You can also ask it to seperate different parts of an image, so say "remove everything except the bottom row of trees" and it does that excellently, and you can now use those trees as a new sprite so characters can walk under it.

The basic flow is to get it to generate a sprite, either totally new or by reference image (which works great!), then you take that sprite and tell it to animate it with parameters for frames, duration and few other things.

Once you are happy with the animations you can tell it to create new directions like facing the camera.  Voila, full sprite sheets of an animated character.

Issues I've come across are that sometimes it just slams your reference image in the middle for no reason, which you can easily remove in the editor by just telling it to.  Like I said any paths that aren't flat 2d are going to give you headaches.  And promoting complex or vague alterations to an image usually makes things progressively worse and you get very strange results - you're better off to just keep spamming new images.

There are also options to add/remove apparel to sprites, and I am assuming would work for weapons that they hold, but I haven't tried that yet.

All the common styles of art and perspective are built-in and work great, but some unique looking stuff takes some exacting prompts and a few attempts.  Once you have the style though you use those images as references and it carries over very nicely.

Cost wise: the free version is enough to do just a couple of animations and that's it.  Pro is about $50 a month and you can do quite a few fully animated characters and all still images are free, so you can really hone the concepts before animating them.

If you have a look and find that there's something better let me know!

replies.author: jediwhiteshark
replies.body: Can you provide reference points for the character in order to generate sprites? Like "x is where the feet are supposed to be".

replies.author: Suspicious_Bet3623
replies.body: I haven't really tried exactly that, only things like "put a tree next to the house.".  I'll give it a go and let you know how it goes.

replies.author: Suspicious_Bet3623
replies.body:
Yeah it works, but not great. 

 When I asked it to just put a coloured shape somewhere it was perfect, and normal stuff like a helmet on his head was fine.

But when I asked it to do some odd stuff like put an eye patch on his right hand, it did, but also put one on his eye for no reason.  

And once things start going silly they don't stop and are seemingly impossible to correct, you have to revert to a previous version.

I'm sure making detailed, well specified prompts would get better results, as would making a sketch and telling it to put X in Y position (I did that with some maps), but it seems like a limitation.

replies.author: jediwhiteshark
replies.body: With Pixellab, can I provide an incomplete sprite palette and ask it to enhance by adding more frame to it, eg. Add climbing frames for the character etc ?

comments.author: lenorexotica
comments.body:
What I did to make it consistent, if you can’t sketch skip the first step.

1.	⁠sketched my own character on paper.  
2.	⁠upload the image to qwen or ChatGPT to create multi angle character sheet with no words or letters.  
3.	⁠download a reference 1 sheet character animations and use photoshop or affinity, align your layer in top and draw stick figures poses, how you want them. Use the reference, export only the blank background with stick figure poses.  
4.	⁠use qwen or i2i workflow, image 1 use stick figure poses, image 2 use character sheet you created earlier, using image 1 for pose references. Generate the output.  
5.	⁠you can now use this new animation sheet with your character and can loop the process to add effects and customisation.
